title: School Quality and Black-White Relative Earnings: A Direct Assessment
research_question: Did improvements in the relative quality of schools attended by Black students compared to White students contribute to the convergence of Black-White earnings among men born in the southern United States during the first half of the twentieth century? How much of the narrowing earnings gap can be attributed to changes in measurable school characteristics versus other factors?
data_description: The analysis links individual-level earnings data for adult men from the U.S. Census to state-level measures of public school quality in the segregated South. Earnings and demographic information are drawn from Census records covering cohorts of Black and White men born between roughly 1910 and 1950 in southern states, observed in adulthood. School quality measures—including pupil-teacher ratios, term length, and relative teacher salaries—are compiled separately for Black and White schools by state and cohort from historical state education reports. The unit of observation is the individual worker, with school-quality variables matched by state of birth and birth cohort. Outcomes include weekly or annual earnings, with controls for education, region of residence, and experience.
institutional_context: During the first half of the twentieth century, southern U.S. states operated racially segregated 'separate-but-equal' public school systems in which resources allocated to Black schools were systematically inferior to those allocated to White schools. Over successive birth cohorts from the 1910s through the 1950s, the gaps in measurable inputs—such as pupil-teacher ratios, length of the school term, and teacher pay—between Black and White schools narrowed substantially, though at different rates across states. Because cohorts born in different states and years were exposed to markedly different relative school qualities before entering the labor market, this setting provides variation in the educational resources available to Black versus White children that can be related to later labor-market outcomes. The period also coincided with broader changes in labor markets and civil rights conditions affecting Black workers.
